power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Oropouche virus (OROV) causes recurrent outbreaks in South America, including Colombia.
Although Culicoides paraensis is the principal recognized urban vector, the potential involvement of other Culicoides species remains incompletely understood.
In Colombia, studies combining viral detection, host-feeding behavior, and ecological suitability are scarce.
We investigated Culicoides communities in urban and peri-urban environments of Puerto Carreño, Vichada, during two seasonal transitions.
Species identification combined morphology and COI DNA barcoding, and blood-meal sources were identified using vertebrate molecular markers.

OROV RNA was assessed by RT-qPCR targeting the L and S genomic segments, and maximum likelihood prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals were calculated accounting for unequal pool sizes, including a conservative estimate.

Arboviruses pose a major public health threat as they can shift from zoonotic and sylvatic cycles to rural and urban transmission, driven by climate change, unplanned urbanization, human mobility, and land use change [1, 2].

text.text: OROV, a member of the family Peribunyaviridae and genus Orthobunyavirus, possesses a tripartite negativesense RNA genome with segments classified as small (S), medium (M), and large (L).

The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, the M segment encodes glycoproteins involved in viral entry together with the non-structural protein NSm, and the S segment encodes the nucleoprotein and the interferon antagonist NSs [1].

text.text: This segmented genome allows genetic reassortment, an important mechanism of evolution in orthobunyaviruses [9].

text.text: Molecular assays targeting the L segment and the N gene within the S segment are used for OROV detection [10, 11], while sequencing of viral genomic fragments can support identification and provide information on their relationships with reference strains.

text.text: Although C. paraensis has long been considered the primary urban vector, expanding geographic reports of OROV transmission raise the possibility that additional vector species may participate in local transmission cycles in distinct ecological contexts [12, 13].

text.text: Although several mosquito species (family Culicidae) have been investigated as potential OROV vectors, Culicoides paraensis, a biting midge in the family Ceratopogonidae, remains the principal recognized urban vector.
Experimental studies have also demonstrated susceptibility of Culicoides sonorensis to OROV under laboratory conditions [7, 13, 14].

text.text: Culicoides are hematophagous dipterans of the family Ceratopogonidae, whose minute size (<2 mm), cryptic species complexes, and wide distribution complicate their study.

text.text: Their diverse breeding habitats, including muddy soils, marshes, riverbanks, manure, and decaying matter [21, 22], make surveillance and control difficult.

text.text: Given these biological characteristics, distinguishing the Culicoides species that may contribute to OROV transmission requires an approach that integrates taxonomy, viral detection and sequence characterization, and ecological context.
Such integrative strategies are particularly important in regions where entomological data are sparse, and surveillance systems may underestimate viral circulation.

In Colombia, OROV circulation has been documented in the Amazon and border areas with Venezuela, During 2024-2025, 26 human OROV cases were included in the national epidemiological records compiled for this study, while the co-circulation of two viral lineages was documented in the Colombian Amazon in 2024 [8][23], but the Culicoides species potentially involved in local transmission remain poorly characterized.

text.text: National research efforts on Culicoides have largely focused on their nuisance role, leaving major gaps in knowledge regarding species distribution, host-use patterns, and vector potential for arboviruses [24, 25].

text.text: Vichada, with its mosaic of savannas, rainforests, and extensive hydrographic network, combined with socioeconomic dynamics linked to migration and land-use change [26, 27], constitutes a strategic setting for investigating the contribution of Culicoides to OROV transmission.

text.text: In this study, we aimed to characterize Culicoides species in urban and peri-urban areas of Puerto Carreño using an integrated approach combining morphological and molecular taxonomy, host-feeding analysis, and OROV RNA detection.
We also evaluated species-specific ecological suitability and spatial concordance with reported OROV cases.
Together, these analyses provide complementary evidence to prioritize candidate species for experimental vector competence studies and inform entomovirological surveillance of OROV in Colombia.

The study was conducted in the municipality of Puerto Carreño, the capital of the Vichada Department, Colombia, within the Orinoquía ecoregion at the confluence of the Meta and Orinoco rivers (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The study was conducted in the municipality of Puerto Carreño, the capital of the Vichada Department, Colombia, within the Orinoquía ecoregion at the confluence of the Meta and Orinoco rivers (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: This zone between the Orinoquía and Amazon Basin encompasses a complex mosaic of seasonally flooded savannas, morichales (palm-dominated wetlands), gallery forests, and temporary and permanent wetlands interconnected by an extensive hydrographic network [28].

text.text: Collections were conducted during two seasonal transition periods: rainy-to-dry (August-September 2024) and dry-to-rainy (May 2025).
The sampling units corresponded to individual urban or rural households.
At each site, two to five CDC ultraviolet light traps (model CDC 2506N, Curtis Dyna-Fog's Ltd., USA) were deployed according to property size.

Traps were placed both indoors and within 10 m of the dwelling, with placement determined by local land use and nearby habitats likely to host Culicoides breeding or aggregation sites, such as stagnant water organic matter accumulation (e.g., lagoons and banana crops when present), animal enclosures (pigsties, stables, chicken coops), and human living spaces.
The traps were operated for two consecutive nights at each site (17:00-08:00), and collection containers were retrieved each morning.
Each trap-night was considered an independent sampling unit; therefore, a trap operated for two consecutive nights contributed two trap-nights.
After each sampling round, traps were relocated to new households meeting the same selection criteria.
When unusually high midge abundance was recorded at a specific location, additional collections were undertaken during the same fieldwork session.
Capture abundance was standardized by the number of trap-nights to account descriptively for differences in trapping effort between sampling campaigns.

Because sampling effort was unequal and collection sites were selected non-randomly, these standardized values were used to describe capture patterns rather than to infer seasonal changes in Culicoides abundance.
Sampling completeness was assessed through rarefaction analysis performed in R, using site-level species counts standardized by trap per night.
Rarefaction curves enabled the estimation of species richness and evaluation of capture effort across sites, minimizing bias associated with unequal efforts.
Specimens were transported to the Vichada Departmental Public Health Laboratory and chilled at -20 °C for approximately 2 h to induce temporary immobilization.
Samples were sorted to retain Culicoides specimens, which were then separated into morphospecies using taxonomic keys [29] [30] [31] [32] [33] [34] [35].

text.text: Thus, individual morphological sorting preceded pooling, with representative specimens retained individually for taxonomic and molecular identification, blood-fed females separated for host-feeding analysis, and the remaining individuals pooled for viral RNA detection.
Representative specimens of each morphospecies were preserved individually in RNAlater (Invitrogen) for nucleic acid stabilization.

Blood-fed females were kept separately for blood meal source analysis, whereas the remaining individuals were grouped into pools of up to 60 specimens by species, collection date, and site for viral detection assays.
All materials were shipped on dry ice to the Virology Group facilities at Universidad El Bosque (Bogotá, D.C., Colombia) and stored at -80 °C until downstream laboratory processing.
Representative specimens were processed using an integrative taxonomic approach to maintain morphological integrity and downstream suitability.
Specimens were cleared in heated 85% lactic acid and dissected under glycerin.
The mounts were examined using a Primo Star compound microscope and a Stemi 508 stereomicroscope (ZEISS), coupled to an Axiocam ERc 5s camera.
Diagnostic structures, including the head, wings, and male or female terminalia, were mounted and examined in detail for species identification using dichotomous keys and regional monographs.
Voucher specimens were preserved in glycerin-filled tubes as institutional reference material.
Total DNA was extracted from individuals preserved in RNAlater using a commercial column-based kit (IBI Scientific, IB47222), according to manufacturer instructions.

Prior to extraction, samples were mechanically homogenized with sterile plastic pestles in 1.5 mL microtubes containing DEPC-treated water, and then incubated for 2 h in the provided lysis buffer at room temperature for complete tissue digestion.
DNA purity and yield were verified spectrophotometrically using a NanoPhotometer N120.

The genetic diversity and spatial population structure of Culicoides insignis, the most abundant species in the collections and the one most frequently represented in the NCBI database, were examined.
A haplotype network was constructed to visualize relationships among C. insignis COI haplotypes and their geographic distribution.
Each haplotype is represented as a colored node, with connecting branches denoting single mutational steps.
The COI sequences generated in this study were combined with georeferenced C. insignis sequences retrieved from GenBank®.
Alignment was performed using MEGA v11, and the resulting dataset was exported in NEXUS/PAUP format.
Haplotype definition was assigned by locality in DNA Sequence Polymorphism (DnaSP) v6.12.03 and PopArt v1.7 using the minimum spanning haplotype network algorithm.
This approach enabled comparison of local haplotypes with those reported from other regions across the Neotropical range of Culicoides insignis.

text.text: Gradient PCR assays were first calibrated with control blood samples from human, chicken, and duck hosts to define the optimal annealing conditions.
Universal vertebrate primers and human-specific primers (Table 1) were used sequentially to detect single or mixed blood meal sources.

text.text: Each reaction was performed in a final volume of 20 µL, containing 1× qScript PCR Kit (QuantaBio), 0.4 µM of forward and reverse primers, 1 µL of genomic DNA, and nuclease-free water.
PCR products were resolved by electrophoresis on 2% agarose gels and documented using a gel imaging system.
Extracted DNA from uninfected C6/36 Aedes albopictus cell line and from a Culicoides male were used as negative controls, while nuclease-free water was used as a reaction control.
Samples displaying amplicons of the expected size and sufficient intensity were purified and subjected to Sanger sequencing.
The same samples were evaluated using both the universal vertebrate primers and the human-specific primers.
The resulting chromatograms were edited in MEGA v12.0.11, and sequence identity was confirmed through BLASTn searches against the NCBI GenBank database.
Host species were assigned based on a ≥ 98% sequence identity.
This approach enabled the direct identification of vertebrate feeding sources and assessment of potential vector-host associations.
Viral RNA detection was assessed in pools of female Culicoides.
Pool size varied according to species, collection site, and sampling date, ranging from 2 to 60 individuals.
Specimens were preserved immediately after collection in RNAlater to maintain RNA integrity under remote field conditions.
RNA extracted from the pools was initially screened for OROV using two independent one-step RT-qPCR assays targeting the L and S genomic segments (Table 1).

text.text: OROV RNA was extracted from infected cell culture supernatants denominated LET-01 and LET-05, in separate laboratory areas and biosafety cabinets from those used for the field-collected Culicoides samples.
During RT-qPCR setup, positive-control templates were added last, after the sample tubes had been placed in the thermocycler.
RNA extracted from uninfected C6/36 Aedes albopictus cells served as a negative extraction control, and nuclease-free water was included as a no-template control in each run.
Because pool sizes varied among samples, OROV prevalence was estimated using a pooled-binomial maximum likelihood approach that explicitly accounts for individual pool sizes.

Estimates and 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the pooledBin function in the R package binGroup (v2.2.3), with the maximum likelihood estimator and skew-score confidence intervals and are reported per 1,000 individuals.
Estimates were calculated separately for the L and S molecular targets and, using a more conservative criterion, for pools showing concordant positivity for both targets.
This criterion reflects the concurrent detection of two genomic segments in Culicoides species not previously characterized in this context.
Samples were selected for amplicon sequencing using the Oxford Nanopore platform based on RNA availability and RT-qPCR results.
Samples with Cq values below 36 for either target and samples positive for both the L and S targets were prioritized for sequencing.
Multiplex amplification was performed using primer sets targeting L, M, and S (Table 1) genomic segments.
text.formatted: Multiplex amplification was performed using primer sets targeting L, M, and S (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>) genomic segments.

text.text: Sequencing reads were filtered by length (250-800 bp) and mapped independently against OROV reference sequences using Minimap2 with settings optimized for Oxford Nanopore reads.
Only primary alignments with a mapping quality (MAPQ) ≥20 were retained for downstream analyses.
Read-derived consensus sequences were reconstructed independently for each sample and genomic region.

Positions with a minimum read depth of 10× were retained, and the nucleotide supported by the 70% of reads at each position was incorporated into the consensus sequence; positions with equal support for alternative nucleotides were coded as ambiguous (N).
Reference nucleotides were not used to fill uncovered or insufficiently supported positions, and discontinuous regions of coverage were retained as independent fragments.
Negative controls were included during the Nanopore sequencing workflow to monitor potential contamination during library preparation and sequencing.
To assess sequence concordance and potential laboratory-source similarity, field-derived consensus sequences were compared with OROV control sequences generated independently by Sanger sequencing.
Comparisons were restricted to homologous overlapping regions and included calculation of nucleotide identity and identification of nucleotide differences.
For discrepant positions, nucleotide calls in the Nanopore consensus were evaluated against the underlying mapped-read data, including read depth, nucleotide counts, and majority-allele frequency.

Pairwise genetic distances were calculated as uncorrected p-distances, representing the proportion of nucleotide differences across homologous positions, with gaps and ambiguous nucleotides excluded pairwise.
Distances were calculated separately among field-derived sequences and between fieldderived sequences and laboratory controls for the L (173 nt), M (316 nt), and S (299 nt) segments.
For the extended M-segment dataset (656 nt), distances between B76/B82 and publicly available reference sequences were calculated and summarized according to previously assigned phylogenetic groups.

For phylogenetic analyses, Nanopore-derived consensus sequences were aligned with publicly available OROV sequences representing the genetic diversity of the corresponding genomic segments from GISAID up to September 30, 2026.
Alignments were constructed separately for the L, M, and S segments and restricted to homologous genomic regions; non-overlapping fragments were not concatenated.
The 13 field-derived sequences were initially aligned separately for each genomic segment.

For phylogenetic analyses, sequence subsets were selected according to fragment length and the availability of homologous regions in the reference sequences, aiming to retain the largest possible number of samples while maintaining a sufficiently long region for comparison.
Because fragment lengths varied among samples, separate alignments were generated for some segments.
For the M segment, two alignments covering the same genomic region but differing in sequence length and sample inclusion were analyzed.
Most S-segment fragments were approximately 90 bp long and were excluded from phylogenetic analysis when their limited length did not allow meaningful comparison with reference sequences.
Nucleotide substitution models were evaluated using IQ-TREE 2, and Bayesian phylogenetic inference was performed in MrBayes using the selected segment-specific models.

Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses were run for 5 × 10⁶ generations, with convergence evaluated using the average standard deviation of split frequencies, effective sample sizes, and potential scale reduction factors.
Node support was expressed as posterior probabilities.
Phylogenetic placement of field-derived sequences was evaluated in the context of publicly available OROV sequences and previously reported phylogenetic group assignments.

text.text: Records were curated to remove duplicates, spatial outliers, and entries that lacked precise geographic coordinates.
Only georeferenced records with adequate spatial resolution were retained.

Because the objective was to compare species-specific environmental structuring at a continental scale rather than to produce fine-resolution predictive maps, occurrence records were subjected to quality control before ecological niche modeling.
Records with missing or invalid geographic coordinates, exact duplicate coordinate pairs, and locations outside the predefined geographic extent of the Americas (120°W-30°W; 60°S-35°N) were excluded.
Occurrences with missing values for the environmental predictors retained in each species-specific model were also removed.
No minimum-distance spatial thinning was applied; therefore, geographically proximate records with distinct coordinates could remain in the final occurrence datasets.
Environmental predictors representing climatic, topographic, vegetational, and edaphic attributes were obtained from publicly available global datasets.

Bioclimatic variables (BIO1-BIO19), representing long-term summaries of temperature and precipitation, were downloaded from WorldClim v2.1 (1970-2000 normals; https://www.worldclim.org/) at 30 arc-second (~1 km) resolution.

text.text: The mean annual wind speed at a height of 10 m was derived from the WorldClim monthly climate layers.

Elevation data were obtained from NASADEM_HGT/001 (https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/), and soil conditions were represented by the soil organic carbon content in the upper 0-5 cm layer from SoilGrids (https://soilgrids.org/).
text.formatted: Elevation data were obtained from NASADEM_HGT/001 (<ref type="url" target="https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/">https://lpdaac.usgs.gov), and the terrain slope was computed using QGIS. Vegetation   productivity was characterized using long-term MODIS MOD13 products (https://lpdaac.usgs.gov</ref>), and soil conditions were represented by the soil organic carbon content in the upper 0-5 cm layer from SoilGrids (<ref type="url" target="https://soilgrids.org/">https://soilgrids.org</ref>).

text.text: All raster layers were resampled and harmonized to a spatial resolution of ~ 1 km in WGS84 (EPSG:4326) and clipped to a continental extent encompassing the documented biogeographic distribution of the studied taxa across the Americas (120°W to 30°W; 60°S to 35°N) prior to export from Google Earth Engine.
Species distribution models were implemented in R (v4.5.1) using the maximum entropy algorithm (Maxnet package) and spatial raster tools from the terra package.
Multicollinearity among environmental predictors was assessed independently for each species using the variance inflation factor (VIF).

A threshold of VIF ≤ 10 was applied to identify and exclude highly collinear predictors, following established methodological criteria commonly used in ecological modeling and species distribution studies.
For each species, a target of 2,000 background points was specified within the modeling extent.

However, the effective number of background points used in model fitting varied among species, as determined by the species-specific modeling datasets and the availability of environmental information.
The final number of background points used for each species is reported in Table 5.
text.formatted: The final number of background points used for each species is reported in Table <ref type="table">5</ref>.

text.text: For each species, occurrence records were randomly partitioned into training (70%) and testing (30%) subsets, without spatial stratification.
Habitat suitability surfaces were projected using a cloglog transformation.

The modeling extent was defined to encompass the maximum documented geographic distributions reported for the studied taxa in previous systematic and faunistic studies, particularly for Culicoides insignis, thereby avoiding extrapolation beyond its known continental range.
Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and the True Skill Statistic (TSS), calculated on independent test data (pROC package).
Binary suitability maps were derived using thresholds that maximized the sensitivity and specificity (Youden's index).
Variable importance was quantified using a drop-AUC approach, in which each retained predictor was sequentially removed, and the resulting reduction in AUC in the test data was recorded.
Predictors yielding positive drop-AUC values were interpreted as having independent explanatory contributions ("effective predictors").
To evaluate interspecific ecological similarity, pairwise Jaccard similarity indices were calculated based on the presence or absence of effective predictors for each species in the study.
This metric quantifies shared, independently informative environmental drivers rather than spatial niche overlap.

Final suitability maps were generated for Culicoides insignis, C. pusillus, C. ignacioi, and C. paraensis to compare the ecological structuring and potential geographic overlap among potential Oropouche virus epidemiological interest Culicoides species.

To assess the spatial concordance between predicted Culicoides species suitability and reported human OROV cases, species-specific suitability maps were overlaid with reported case distributions to visualize spatial cooccurrence patterns across the Americas.
A fixed suitability threshold (≥ 0.4) was used to define highsuitability areas.

This value approximated the range of species-specific optimal discrimination thresholds derived from model performance metrics and was consistently applied across taxa to enable standardized interspecific comparisons.
The suitable areas were derived from Maxent models and projected as continuous cloglog outputs.

Reported human OROV case data were compiled from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO/WHO) and national surveillance reports from Brazil (11,888 cases), Panama (501), Peru (330), Colombia (26), Cuba (28), Venezuela (5), and Guyana (1) [8, 11].

text.text: For all countries except Venezuela (where data were available only at the national level), cases were assigned to first-order administrative units (e.g., departments or provinces).
To formally evaluate administrative-scale ecological concordance, suitability values were summarized within each first-order administrative unit by calculating the mean suitability.
Differences between regions with and without reported OROV cases were assessed using Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

In addition, suitability values were dichotomized using a fixed threshold (≥ 0.4) to generate binary high/low suitability categories, which were cross-tabulated against case presence to compute odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals using Fisher's exact test.

Of these, 1,618 individuals were captured during the transition from rainy-to-dry weather, whereas 21 were collected during the transition from dry-to-rainy weather.
Specimens were assigned to 11 morphologically defined taxa.

00 Specimens identified based on wing patterns, genitalia, and head morphology as C. leopoldoi, C. pusillus, C. 01 ignacioi, and C. foxi each clustered with their respective reference sequences in well-supported nodes, 02 corroborating morphological assignments and supporting the utility of COI as a DNA barcode marker for 03 species-level delimitation in these taxa.
Specimens morphologically assigned to C. venezuelensis and 04 additional taxa did not yield high-quality consensus sequences and were therefore excluded from phylogenetic 05 reconstruction.

In contrast, morphotypes designated as C. cf. insinuatus and C. cf. todatangae grouped within the broader clade corresponding to the C. paraensis species complex and other members of the subgenus Haematomyidium, consistent with their diagnostic morphological affinity.
However, no confidently identified reference sequences for these exact taxa were available for direct comparison.
Additionally, C. daviesi formed a distinct lineage within the Mataemyia group, for which no other reference sequences were available in GenBank.
Pairwise COI genetic distances (K2P) further supported these phylogenetic patterns.

Intraspecific divergence was low to moderate across taxa, including C. foxi (0.6-1.1%), C. ignacioi (0.3-2.0%), C. insignis (0.3-4.0%), C. cf. insinuatus (0.3-2.3%), C. leopoldoi (1.7%), and C. pusillus (2.3-4.3%).
In contrast, interspecific divergence between C. ignacioi and the reference C. guttatus sequence was high (16-17%), supporting their molecular separation despite superficial morphological similarity.
Distances within Culicoides cf. todatangae were low (0.6%), consistent with close relatedness between the two specimens.

For the lineage assigned as Culicoides daviesi intraspecific divergence was 1.1%, whereas interspecific distances ranged from 16.9-17.3% relative to C. insinuatus, 17-20% relative to C. paraensis, and 17-19% relative to C. galindoi.

To further explore the genetic diversity of Culicoides insignis, the predominant species in Puerto Carreño, we analyzed the distribution of COI haplotypes obtained in this study together with previously reported sequences from other regions of the Americas.
The network showed a compact topology, with most haplotypes separated by relatively few mutational steps and no apparent deep divergence among the sampled haplotypes (Figure 3).

51 A total of 64 blood-fed females were analyzed, including C. insignis (n = 56), C. ignacioi (n = 2), C. pusillus 52 (n = 5), and C. foxi (n = 1).
Three vertebrate blood-meal sources were identified: Homo sapiens (14% of 53 analyzed specimens), Equus caballus (36%), and Sus scrofa (8%).
These sources were identified in C. insignis, 54 with horses being the most frequently detected host, followed by humans and pigs.
Mixed blood meals 55 involving humans and horses were also detected in six C. insignis specimens.
Equine blood was additionally 56 detected in C. foxi and C. ignacioi, whereas C. pusillus specimens showed evidence of feeding on humans and 57 horses.
These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small number of specimens analyzed for 58 species other than C. insignis (Table 3).

text.text: The presence of OROV RNA was assessed by RT-qPCR targeting partial fragments of the L and S genomic segments in pooled specimens.
The results are summarized in Table 4.
text.formatted: The results are summarized in Table <ref type="table">4</ref>.

text.text: Culicoides insignis showed the highest number of positive pools, with L segment amplification detected in 30 of 52 pools (57.7%) comprising 1,283 individuals.
Accounting for unequal pool sizes, the estimated prevalence was 37.37 per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 25.69-51.96).

Detection using the S-segment assay was less frequent, with 7 of 44 pools (15.9%) testing positive among 1,111 individuals, corresponding to an estimated prevalence of 6.71 per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 2.99-12.86).

When a more conservative criterion requiring concordant detection of both genomic targets was applied, 3 of 32 pools were positive among 882 individuals, resulting in an estimated prevalence of 3.61 per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 0.94-9.60).
Interestingly, OROV RNA was detected in two females without visible blood remnants that also tested negative in blood-meal PCR assays.
Thus, no evidence of a recent blood meal was detected in these specimens, and at least one positive C. insignis specimen was collected in an urban setting.

OROV L-segment RNA was also detected in C. pusillus, with four of six pools testing positive among 24 individuals, corresponding to an estimated prevalence of 371.01 per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 104.71-757.96).
No S-segment amplification was detected in the three C. pusillus pools evaluated with this assay, and none of the pools evaluated for both targets showed concordant positivity.
In C. ignacioi, both pools evaluated for the L segment were positive, representing five individuals; however, prevalence could not be reliably estimated because all evaluated pools were positive.
One of four pools evaluated for the S segment was positive, corresponding to an estimated prevalence of 87.13 per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 5.13-317.53).
The only C. ignacioi pool evaluated for both targets was positive for both L and S, but the very small sample size 83 precluded a reliable prevalence estimate.

Because C. pusillus and C. ignacioi were represented by few 84 individuals and pools, these estimates were highly uncertain and should not be interpreted as evidence of 85 higher OROV prevalence than that observed in C. insignis.

text.text: Viral detection was based on RT-qPCR targeting the L and S segments and, in selected positive pools, was further supported by targeted Nanopore sequencing, which recovered OROV-specific sequences from all three genomic segments.
Culicoides species with molecular evidence of OROV infection were associated with multiple vertebrate hosts, including humans, pigs, and horses.

C. insignis showed the highest connectivity, reflecting its frequent viral detection and broader range of identified blood-meal sources, whereas C. pusillus and C. ignacioi showed fewer host associations.
Overall, the network provides a descriptive integration of the virological and blood-meal findings across the three Culicoides species.

Model performance was moderate to high (AUC = 0.74-0.92; TSS = 0.56-0.68), with C. pusillus showing the strongest discrimination (AUC = 0.92; TSS = 0.68) (Table 5).

text.text: C. ignacioi, modeled with the smallest cleaned occurrence dataset (n = 16), exhibited three effective predictors, primarily annual temperature range (BIO07; drop-AUC = 0.03), slope, and precipitation seasonality (BIO15).
Model performance was comparatively lower (AUC = 0.74; TSS = 0.59), and the limited number of occurrence records restrict further interpretation of its environmental associations.
C. insignis showed six effective predictors and moderate to high discrimination capacity (AUC = 0.87; TSS = 0.56).

Elevation emerged as highest-ranked predictor (drop-AUC = 0.02), followed by isothermality (BIO03), precipitation during the warmest quarter (BIO18), wind speed, and BIO10, indicating contributions from both climatic and topographic variables (Table 5).

text.text: Although C. paraensis and C. pusillus both retained eight effective predictors, their ecological configurations differed.

In C. paraensis, isothermality (BIO03; drop-AUC = 0.06) was the dominant contributor, with additional effects from precipitation metrics (BIO08, BIO13, BIO18) and soil-related variables, indicating contributions from temperature and precipitation-related variables.

In contrast, C. pusillus displayed a more distributed contribution pattern, with BIO03 (drop-AUC = 0.03), elevation, BIO08, slope, and BIO19 contributing independently, indicating a different combination of informative environmental predictors (Table 5).

text.text: C. paraensis showed the clearest positive association between suitability and reported case occurrence, but without significant statistical association.

In contrast, C. insignis displayed a broad and continuous pattern of suitability extending across northern South America, the Brazilian Atlantic coast, and Caribbean regions, including areas with limited or no reported case intensity.
Predicted suitable areas extended beyond regions with historically documented OROV transmission.
Suitability for C. pusillus and C. ignacioi showed partial overlap with regions reporting OROV cases in Brazil and the Amazon basin but also extended into areas with few or no reported cases.

Overall, the maps indicate partial spatial concordance rather than strict geographic coincidence between environmental suitability and reported OROV cases, with substantial areas of predicted suitability occurring outside documented outbreak regions.

To assess macro-scale ecological concordance between predicted suitability and reported OROV cases, mean suitability values were compared across first-level administrative units with and without confirmed cases.

Among the four species evaluated, only C. paraensis showed the clearest positive association between suitability and reported case occurrence, although neither statistical test reached significance (Wilcoxon W = 6108, p = 0.059).

Binary concordance analysis using a suitability threshold ≥ 0.4 indicated increased odds of case occurrence in suitable areas (OR = 2.03, 95% CI 0.74-5.05; Fisher's exact p = 0.119), although this association did not reach statistical significance.

Suitability distributions also differed between administrative units with and without reported cases for C. ignacioi (W = 10862, p = 0.046), but without significant binary concordance (OR = 0.64, 95% CI 0.27-1.52; p = 0.307).
No evidence of concordance was detected for C. pusillus (W = 7838, p = 0.990; OR = 0.19, 95% CI 0.004-1.17; p = 0.104).

For C. insignis, administrative units with suitability ≥ 0.4 did not overlap with reported case regions, resulting in a negative association in binary analysis (OR = 0, 95% CI 0-0.79; p = 0.023), although continuous suitability distributions did not differ significantly (W = 8148, p = 0.723).
Overall, associations between predicted environmental suitability and reported human OROV cases varied among species and between analytical approaches.

C. paraensis showed the most consistent direction of positive association, although statistical support was limited, whereas the remaining species showed weak, inconsistent, or negative associations at an administrative scale.

This study integrates taxonomic, trophic, virological, and ecological approaches to characterize Culicoides communities and their potential relevance to OROV ecology in an understudied region of Colombia.

Morphological identification supported by COI barcoding documented local species diversity, while RT-qPCR and targeted sequencing provided molecular evidence of OROV RNA in C. insignis, C. pusillus, and C. ignacioi.
Blood-meal analysis identified vertebrate hosts used by these species, and ecological niche models characterized their environmental associations across the Americas.

Together, these findings provide speciesspecific evidence to guide entomovirological surveillance and prioritize further investigations into the potential involvement of Culicoides species in OROV transmission.
Applying an integrative taxonomic framework proved particularly informative for Culicoides, a genus characterized by subtle morphological differentiation and frequent cryptic species complexes.
Reliance on a single line of evidence can lead to misidentifications and underestimation of diversity [17, 47].

text.text: This study generated the first COI sequence dataset for Culicoides species from Colombia.

Phylogenetic analyses revealed well-resolved clades for C. insignis, C. ignacioi, C. foxi and C. pusillus, largely consistent with morphological identifications based on wing, head, and genital characters.

However, several morphotypes did not cluster with available reference sequences or form monophyletic groups, highlighting the need to report barcode sequences for neotropical Culicoides species, as their morphological and genetic diversity remains incompletely characterized.

Species richness was lower than that reported in sylvatic and peridomestic areas of the Brazilian Amazon [34], but slightly higher than that documented in rural areas with livestock in Brazil, Peru, and Argentina in studies with comparable sampling approaches [48, 49].
text.formatted: Species richness was lower than that reported in sylvatic and peridomestic areas of the Brazilian Amazon <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[34]</ref>, but slightly higher than that documented in rural areas with livestock in Brazil, Peru, and Argentina in studies with comparable sampling approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">49]</ref>.

text.text: The community was strongly dominated by Culicoides insignis, accounting for over 70% of specimens and present at most sites.
Similar dominance has been reported in Peru [49] and Argentina [50], supporting its characterization as synanthropic and ecologically tolerant.
text.formatted: Similar dominance has been reported in Peru <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[49]</ref> and Argentina <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[50]</ref>, supporting its characterization as synanthropic and ecologically tolerant.

text.text: The marked intraspecific genetic variation observed in C. insignis is consistent with the diversity reported for widely distributed Culicoides species [51, 52].
text.formatted: The marked intraspecific genetic variation observed in C. insignis is consistent with the diversity reported for widely distributed Culicoides species <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[51,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">52]</ref>.

text.text: Although its geographic and population-level structure requires further investigation.
The exclusive use of CDC light traps may have underrepresented C. paraensis, as human-attraction methods have shown higher collection efficiency for this species in other settings [53].

text.text: Molecular detection of OROV RNA in multiple Culicoides species provides evidence of the presence of the viral RNA in local midge populations.

In C. insignis, prevalence estimates varied substantially according to the molecular criterion used, with the estimate based on concordant detection of both targets being substantially lower than those obtained from either molecular target individually.
Using this more conservative criterion, the estimated prevalence was 3.61 per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 0.94-9.60).
Comparable entomological estimates for OROV remain scarce.

During the 2024 outbreak in Cuba, OROV RNA was detected in one of two Ceratopogonidae pools analyzed, including 14 apparently non-engorged females in the positive pool, although specimens could not be identified to species [54].
text.formatted: During the 2024 outbreak in Cuba, OROV RNA was detected in one of two Ceratopogonidae pools analyzed, including 14 apparently non-engorged females in the positive pool, although specimens could not be identified to species <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[54]</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, recent surveillance in outbreak areas of Minas Gerais, Brazil, detected no OROV-positive pools among 212 C. paraensis or 607 C. leopoldoi [53].
text.formatted: In contrast, recent surveillance in outbreak areas of Minas Gerais, Brazil, detected no OROV-positive pools among 212 C. paraensis or 607 C. leopoldoi <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[53]</ref>.

text.text: These contrasting findings emphasize the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of OROV detection in Culicoides populations and the limited availability of directly comparable entomological infection estimates.

Interestingly, the prevalence estimated using concordant OROV detection in our C. insignis samples is of a similar order of magnitude to the 0.33% (approximately 3.3 per 1,000) BTV infection rate recently reported in unengorged C. insignis from Ecuador [55], although comparisons between different viruses, sampling designs, and analytical approaches should be interpreted cautiously.

text.text: Furthermore, given the recognized role of C. insignis as a candidate vector of bluetongue virus in South America, the environmental conditions associated with its distribution in our models may also be relevant to surveillance of other Culicoides borne arboviruses, although their circulation including other Orthabunyavirus was not assessed in this study.
Although no OROV cases have been officially reported in Vichada, underdiagnosis or clinical misclassification with other febrile illnesses, such as dengue, cannot be excluded [4, 56].
text.formatted: Although no OROV cases have been officially reported in Vichada, underdiagnosis or clinical misclassification with other febrile illnesses, such as dengue, cannot be excluded <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">56]</ref>.

text.text: Detection of both L and S genomic segments in C. insignis, including some unfed females, suggests that viral RNA detection is unlikely to be solely associated with recent blood ingestion, although this does not demonstrate disseminated infection or vector competence.
The marked difference in positivity between the L and S molecular targets highlights the importance of assay-dependent interpretation of OROV RNA detection.
Differences in analytical sensitivity, target-region characteristics, or RNA integrity may have contributed to this discordance.

Wise et al. [57] demonstrated that mismatches between diagnostic primers and an Ecuadorian OROV lineage compromised viral detection, with primer redesign improving analytical sensitivity by up to three orders of magnitude.
text.formatted: Wise et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[57]</ref> demonstrated that mismatches between diagnostic primers and an Ecuadorian OROV lineage compromised viral detection, with primer redesign improving analytical sensitivity by up to three orders of magnitude.

text.text: This highlights how genetic variation in target regions can affect molecular detection and should be considered when interpreting differences between diagnostic targets.

Sequence-based characterization provides an additional level of molecular support for OROV detection in Culicoides and allows these detections to be interpreted within the genetic diversity currently recognized in South America.

Recent genomic surveillance has revealed substantial OROV diversity in South America, including the co-circulation and changing relative frequency of genetically distinct viral populations in the Colombian Amazon [23, 58, 59].
text.formatted: Recent genomic surveillance has revealed substantial OROV diversity in South America, including the co-circulation and changing relative frequency of genetically distinct viral populations in the Colombian Amazon <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">59]</ref>.

text.text: In this context, the phylogenetic proximity of the midge-derived M-segment sequences to sequences associated with the recent outbreak is consistent with contemporary regional OROV diversity.

Importantly, however, the field-derived sequences were not identical to previously reported sequences across the homologous regions analyzed; a pattern observed both for the longer M-segment region and for most of the shorter genomic fragments.

This differentiation may reflect previously unsampled OROV viral diversity, particularly because OROV had not previously been documented or genetically characterized in Vichada, although the limited genomic coverage prevents determining whether these differences represent geographically structured diversity or broader variation among circulating OROV populations.

Recent genomic studies have demonstrated that the evolutionary relationships of OROV may differ among its three genomic segments, and formal assignment of contemporary lineages has relied on complete or nearcomplete genomic information [23, 58, 59].
text.formatted: Recent genomic studies have demonstrated that the evolutionary relationships of OROV may differ among its three genomic segments, and formal assignment of contemporary lineages has relied on complete or nearcomplete genomic information <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">59]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the partial sequences recovered here should not be interpreted as evidence for formal lineage assignment or reassortment.

Instead, they support the genetic characterization of OROV detected in field-collected Culicoides and highlight the need to obtain complete or near-complete viral genomes directly from biting midges to determine how OROV diversity in vectors relates to that characterized from contemporary human infections in Colombia and elsewhere in South America.
Blood meal analysis revealed opportunistic feeding by C. insignis on horses (Equus caballus), humans (Homo sapiens), and pigs (Sus scrofa), consistent with findings from Ecuador [55].
text.formatted: Blood meal analysis revealed opportunistic feeding by C. insignis on horses (Equus caballus), humans (Homo sapiens), and pigs (Sus scrofa), consistent with findings from Ecuador <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[55]</ref>.

text.text: Similar feeding patterns in other hematophagous dipterans in Colombia suggest that shared vertebrate hosts in anthropogenically modified landscapes may facilitate viral spillover [60].
text.formatted: Similar feeding patterns in other hematophagous dipterans in Colombia suggest that shared vertebrate hosts in anthropogenically modified landscapes may facilitate viral spillover <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[60]</ref>.

text.text: Although horses are not currently considered competent amplifying hosts for OROV, serological surveys in Brazil have reported neutralizing or hemagglutinationinhibiting antibodies against orthobunyaviruses in equines [61, 62], indicating exposure in peri-urban and rural settings.

text.text: A central contribution of this study is the comparative ecological characterization of potential epidemiological interest Culicoides species.
Previous niche modeling of C. paraensis emphasized temperature-related variables and precipitation seasonality as dominant drivers of distribution [12].
text.formatted: Previous niche modeling of C. paraensis emphasized temperature-related variables and precipitation seasonality as dominant drivers of distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Our models recover part of this signal, particularly temperature stability (BIO03) and precipitation metrics.
Prior modeling of C. insignis identified temperature, precipitation during the warmest quarter, elevation, and vegetation indices as key predictors [63, 64].
text.formatted: Prior modeling of C. insignis identified temperature, precipitation during the warmest quarter, elevation, and vegetation indices as key predictors <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[63,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">64]</ref>.

text.text: Our results are broadly concordant, with elevation, precipitation variables (BIO18, BIO19), and wind speed emerging as independently informative predictors.
Vegetation and soil variables exerted comparatively minor effects.
Although precipitation did not uniformly dominate model performance, it creates temporary changes in surface moisture, and larval habitat availability [50].
text.formatted: Although precipitation did not uniformly dominate model performance, it creates temporary changes in surface moisture, and larval habitat availability <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[50]</ref>.

text.text: Recent models have further identified humidity, soil moisture, and agricultural land use, particularly banana cultivation, as important correlates of C. paraensis suitability, consistent with the use of decaying banana stems and cocoa residues as larval habitats, while phylogeographic analyses have associated banana and cocoa cultivation, human population density, and C. paraensis suitability with OROV expansion [65, 66].
text.formatted: Recent models have further identified humidity, soil moisture, and agricultural land use, particularly banana cultivation, as important correlates of C. paraensis suitability, consistent with the use of decaying banana stems and cocoa residues as larval habitats, while phylogeographic analyses have associated banana and cocoa cultivation, human population density, and C. paraensis suitability with OROV expansion <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[65,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">66]</ref>.

text.text: Environmental predictors identified among Culicoides species in our study, suggest that their ecological associations may be more heterogeneous than those commonly represented in mosquito-centered arbovirus models, highlighting the need to consider multiple vector species and their species-specific habitat requirements.

Wind-driven movement is increasingly recognized as facilitating range expansion and connectivity in Culicoides [67], providing a plausible ecological explanation for the broad geographic distribution and genetic connectivity observed in C. insignis, although its role in shaping the distribution of this species in the study region remains untested.
text.formatted: Wind-driven movement is increasingly recognized as facilitating range expansion and connectivity in Culicoides <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[67]</ref>, providing a plausible ecological explanation for the broad geographic distribution and genetic connectivity observed in C. insignis, although its role in shaping the distribution of this species in the study region remains untested.

text.text: Furthermore, as occurrence records were not spatially thinned, geographic clustering and uneven sampling intensity in biodiversity databases may have influenced model predictions and performance metrics.
Accordingly, the ecological suitability estimates should be interpreted as exploratory, particularly for species represented by relatively few occurrence records.
Spatial comparisons revealed heterogeneous associations between Culicoides predicted suitability and reported OROV cases.
Previous projections for C. paraensis have shown discrepancies with reported Oropouche fever occurrence, interpreted as potential underdetection or involvement of additional vectors [12].
text.formatted: Previous projections for C. paraensis have shown discrepancies with reported Oropouche fever occurrence, interpreted as potential underdetection or involvement of additional vectors <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: This heterogeneity likely reflects the coarse spatial resolution of available epidemiological data and withinunit environmental heterogeneity, where focal high-suitability areas may be diluted when averaged across large administrative regions.
Stronger concordance for C. paraensis aligns with its recognized epidemiological role.

Given the broad environmental suitability predicted for multiple potential epidemiological interest Culicoides species, including C. paraensis, the geographic extent of ecological permissiveness may exceed the currently documented distribution of human cases.

OROV infection presents nonspecific febrile symptoms overlapping with dengue and other arboviral illnesses, increasing the likelihood of underdiagnosis and misclassification in passive surveillance systems [5].
text.formatted: OROV infection presents nonspecific febrile symptoms overlapping with dengue and other arboviral illnesses, increasing the likelihood of underdiagnosis and misclassification in passive surveillance systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, discrepancies were observed between ecological suitability and reported incidence [68].
text.formatted: Moreover, discrepancies were observed between ecological suitability and reported incidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[68]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, reported case occurrence is influenced by surveillance intensity, diagnostic capacity, population density, human mobility, healthcare access, and reporting practices, none of which were explicitly considered in our spatial comparisons; therefore, ecological concordance should not be interpreted as direct evidence of epidemiological relevance or vector involvement.

Taken together, the taxonomic, trophic, virological, and ecological findings support further investigation of Culicoides species other than C. paraensis in the context of OROV circulation in Colombia.

Among the species examined, C. insignis warrants particular attention because of its local abundance, repeated molecular detections of OROV, including in pools of females without detectable blood meals, and evidence of feeding on humans and domestic animals.

OROV-derived sequences were also recovered from C. pusillus and C. ignacioi, although their limited sample sizes and less extensive host-feeding data restrict further interpretation of their epidemiological relevance.
These findings do not establish additional OROV vectors or demonstrate a multi-vector transmission system.
Rather, they identify species for which experimental studies of viral infection, dissemination, and transmission are needed to clarify their potential roles in OROV ecology.

In conclusion, integrating taxonomy, ecology, host-feeding patterns, and virological evidence provides a practical approach to identifying and prioritizing Culicoides species for further investigation in understudied regions.

By generating convergent evidence within the same surveillance framework, this approach moves beyond isolated viral detections and single-species assumptions and enables candidate vectors to be progressively prioritized according to multiple complementary criteria.

Although these findings do not establish additional OROV vectors, they illustrate how integrative entomovirological surveillance can simultaneously detect emerging viruses, characterize their ecological context, and generate the evidence needed to direct vector-competence studies and subsequent vector-incrimination efforts.
